title: Medical Specialty Prediction from Bangla Patient Narratives: A Comparative Study of ML, DL, Transformers, and LLMs
authors: Tasnin Tabassum Ali, Faisal Ahmed, Muhammad Anwarul Azim
abstract: Timely access to appropriate medical specialists remains a bottleneck in Bangladesh's healthcare system, as patients describe symptoms in informal Bangla rather than clinical terms, leading to ineffective referrals. This paper compares four model families for predicting medical specialties from Bangla patient narratives: six machine learning (ML) models using hybrid TF-IDF features, four deep learning (DL) models using Word2Vec embeddings trained on the corpus, four fine-tuned transformers, and five large language models (LLMs) evaluated zero-shot. From a corpus of 3798 patient records covering 20 specialties, we retained the five with the most records (Medicine, Gynecology, Dermatology, Pediatrics, Gastroenterology) and split the resulting 2730 records 80:20 into training and test sets shared by all families. The best transformer was XLM-RoBERTa (86.26% accuracy, 86.21% macro-F1), the best ML model was SVM (84.98%, 84.92%), the best DL model was Bidirectional GRU (80.77%, 80.83%), and the best LLM was Gemini (90.29%, 90.15%). Holm-corrected paired McNemar tests show SVM significantly outperforming Bi-LSTM (adjusted p = 0.004), whereas the Gemini-versus-Grok gap does not survive correction (adjusted p = 0.104), and neither the strongest transformer versus the weakest LLM (Grok) nor SVM versus the strongest transformer reaches significance. A tuned classical model is thus statistically indistinguishable from the strongest transformer, so accuracy rankings alone should not be read as evidence of one family's superiority. The findings provide a comparative baseline for Bangla medical text classification.

infographic.key_insight: Gemini had the highest accuracy (90.29%), but SVM and the strongest transformer did not differ significantly, cautioning against claims of model-family superiority.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Classifying informal Bangla patient narratives could support specialty referral workflows, but clinical benefit and safety remain untested.
method: Compared 6 classical ML, 4 deep learning, 4 fine-tuned transformer, and 5 zero-shot LLM models.
Used 2,730 records across Medicine, Gynecology, Dermatology, Pediatrics, and Gastroenterology with a shared 80:20 train–test split.
Evaluated accuracy, macro-F1, and paired McNemar tests with Holm correction.
infographic.evidence_signal: Best-model accuracies were 90.29% for Gemini, 86.26% for XLM-RoBERTa, 84.98% for SVM, and 80.77% for Bidirectional GRU; the Gemini–Grok difference was not significant after correction.
infographic.watch_item: Evaluation covered only the five most represented specialties from a 20-specialty corpus, limiting generalizability to broader referral settings.
infographic.paper_title: Medical Specialty Prediction from Bangla Patient Narratives: A Comparative Study of ML, DL, Transformers, and LLMs

title: Agentic AI versus pediatric emergency physicians for differential diagnosis of acutely ill and injured children
authors: Georgette, N.; Buckley, T.; Fine, A. M.; Jones, J.; McMurry, A. J.; Geanacopoulos, A.; Genadry, K. C.; Hoffmann, R.; Kahane, C.; Manrai, A. K.; Mandl, K. D.
abstract: BackgroundMisdiagnosis and delayed diagnosis of children in pediatric emergency departments lead to complications, and are particularly problematic in settings with limited pediatric expertise. Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in diagnostic reasoning for adult emergency department patients, but utility for pediatric cases is largely untested. MethodsRetrospective study of patients seen in the emergency department of a major urban pediatric academic medical center and subsequently admitted to the operating room or inpatient service. Records from 100 patients were randomly selected, stratified by age. We compared the accuracy of differential diagnoses (up to five, ranked by likelihood) generated by a previously developed agentic AI system, Dr. CaBot (one configuration with literature search, the other without), with those of four attending pediatric emergency medicine physicians (diagnosticians), all masked to outcome. Encounters were presented to diagnosticians stepwise across four touchpoints: triage, the initial physician evaluation (the a priori primary touchpoint), the full emergency department encounter, and the admission. Ground truth diagnosis was determined by two independent, board-certified pediatric emergency physicians (reviewers) based on the entire clinical encounter. The reviewers, masked to source, then assigned each differential a Bond score (0 to 5; 4 or above was high-scoring). FindingsThe median patient age was 4 years and 41% had a complex chronic condition. Bond score agreement between the two physician reviewers had a weighted kappa of 0.64. For the primary comparison at the initial physician evaluation touchpoint, Dr. CaBot and the diagnosticians both achieved high-scoring differentials in 95% of cases (difference 0%, 95%CI: -5.8, 5.8%). No differences were detected at the other touchpoints. InterpretationDr. CaBot and attending pediatric emergency medicine physicians showed similar performance in generating differential diagnoses from clinical documentation, suggesting potential as a diagnostic aid. Whether this performance can be translated into improvements in care requires prospective evaluation. Research in contextO_ST_ABSEvidence before this studyC_ST_ABSWe searched PubMed using the query ((Pediatric[Title/Abstract]) AND (Emergency medicine[Title/Abstract]) AND ((Artificial Intelligence[Title/Abstract]) OR (Diagnostic reasoning[Title/Abstract]))), for articles published from 1 January 2000 to 31 December 2025, yielding 28 results, of which 16 were deemed not relevant based on title, 6 were reviews not presenting novel data, and 3 were surveys of physician perspectives on artificial intelligence (AI). There were 3 remaining studies of AI applications to pediatric emergency populations. One assessed AI management decisions of critically ill patients. One attempted to automate triage categorization using machine learning. One assessed the diagnostic reasoning of various general large language models (LLMs; e.g. ChatGPT-4o) on adapted cases from a pediatric emergency department in Italy. Overall, there is limited data on the use of specialized AI agents on diagnostic reasoning on real-world pediatric emergency cases. Added value of this studyThe diagnostic accuracy of an LLM-based agentic process was similar to that of four attending pediatric emergency medicine physicians across 100 cases of children evaluated in a pediatric emergency department. Using real world data from electronic health records and a masked multi-physician evaluation of open-ended agentic responses, we demonstrated physician-level accuracy of artificial intelligence in generating differential diagnoses for children. Implications of all the available evidenceThe agent shows promise as a diagnostic aid among children presenting to the emergency department.

infographic.key_insight: At the initial physician evaluation, Dr. CaBot and pediatric emergency physicians both produced high-scoring differential diagnoses in 95% of cases.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Agentic AI may offer diagnostic support in pediatric emergency care, but improved patient outcomes have not been demonstrated.
method: Retrospective study of 100 randomly selected, age-stratified pediatric emergency encounters resulting in admission or surgery.
Compared Dr. CaBot with and without literature search against four attending pediatric emergency physicians across four documentation touchpoints.
Two independent physician reviewers established ground truth and scored differentials while masked to their source.
infographic.evidence_signal: At the prespecified primary touchpoint, the difference in high-scoring differentials was 0 percentage points (95% CI: −5.8 to 5.8); no differences were detected at other touchpoints.
infographic.watch_item: This single-center retrospective documentation study requires prospective validation before conclusions about real-world safety or benefit.
infographic.paper_title: Agentic AI versus pediatric emergency physicians for differential diagnosis of acutely ill and injured children

title: Laya-IsoToken: Day-One Clinical Codebook Switching via Closed-Form Operator Compilation
authors: Zeqiang Wang
abstract: Healthcare systems periodically revise diagnostic and procedural classifications (ICD-9 to ICD-10/11), update hospital reimbursement groupers (MS-DRG), and deploy clinical coding across languages. Supervised coding networks bind clinical text encoders to fixed per-code classifier weights, forcing hospitals to re-annotate tens of thousands of records before switching codebooks, whereas standalone large language models incur high latency and hallucinate invalid codes. Here we show that day-one clinical codebook switching becomes feasible without target-labeled notes when local clinical evidence reading is decoupled from a strictly frozen multilingual concept space. Laya-IsoToken trains a clinical span reader once on source records with zero per-code classifier parameters, separating text evidence from historical disease prevalence. Given only public target code descriptions, closed-form matrix compilation aligns distributional shifts, compensates for paraphrased definitions, and deduplicates sibling codes in under three seconds, while a pre-deployment geometric residual routes unfamiliar concepts to offline language model verification. Across 32,804 MIMIC-IV ICD-9 discharges, Laya-IsoToken matches published supervised baselines (62.6% Micro-F1) while reducing active calibration error by 32%. Switched with zero target training notes to 13,783 unseen-patient ICD-10 discharges, MS-DRG groups, and multilingual cohorts, it outperforms biomedical dense retrievers, semantic crosswalks (+5.4 F1 points on ICD-10, paired $d_z = 0.49$, $p < 0.001$), and official US CMS equivalence mappings (+3.5 points, $p < 0.001$) at 9.4 ms per admission. Pairing this reader with an offline 31B verifier across 1,000 full discharge summaries lifts zero-training ICD-10 coding to 40.6% Micro-F1 (57.0% category F1, $d_z = 0.66$, $p < 0.001$) with 0.0% invalid code hallucinations.

infographic.key_insight: Laya-IsoToken enables clinical codebook switching without target-labeled training notes by separating clinical evidence extraction from code definitions.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could reduce reannotation burdens when hospitals update coding systems, reimbursement groupers, or coding languages.
method: Train a clinical span reader once against a frozen multilingual concept space, with no per-code classifier parameters.
Compile public target code descriptions into alignment operators in under three seconds.
Route unfamiliar concepts to offline language-model verification using a geometric residual.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports 62.6% Micro-F1 on 32,804 ICD-9 discharges, switching to 13,783 unseen-patient ICD-10 discharges without target training notes, and 40.6% ICD-10 Micro-F1 with offline verification on 1,000 summaries.
infographic.watch_item: Reported benchmark performance does not establish deployment readiness; prospective validation across hospitals and assessment of verifier costs remain important.
infographic.paper_title: Laya-IsoToken: Day-One Clinical Codebook Switching via Closed-Form Operator Compilation

title: Learning Multimodal Representations from Partially Paired, Small-Scale Data
authors: Merel Kuijs, Till Richter, Rushin H. Gindra, Korbinian Traeuble, Christian Matek, Rebeka Luknárová
abstract: Modeling multimodal data from partially paired samples is critical for advancing domains like biomedicine, where vast unimodal datasets and foundation models exist but paired data remains scarce. Existing fusion methods rely on large-scale paired datasets, limiting their use in scenarios with incomplete pairing. We introduce CAMEO, an adversarial learning-based modality fusion framework that integrates modalities from small, partially paired datasets. Combining any pre-trained unimodal encoder with a cross-modal latent alignment mechanism, CAMEO learns shared representations requiring only minimal paired samples. Evaluated on computational pathology tasks such as niche classification and cell type composition prediction, CAMEO achieves superior data efficiency, outperforming contrastive approaches like CLIP in low paired-data regimes, and highlighting the benefits of adversarial alignment when paired annotations are scarce. To facilitate further research, we additionally release a fully annotated HuggingFace dataset comprising three organs and paired image and gene expression modalities. By extending fusion methods to address limited pairing and small-scale datasets, we provide a framework that advances multimodal learning and broadens its applicability to real-world biomedical problems.

infographic.key_insight: CAMEO learns shared multimodal representations from small, partially paired datasets, outperforming contrastive approaches such as CLIP when paired data are scarce.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This approach could support computational pathology research combining tissue images and gene expression when matched samples are limited, but clinical utility is not established.
method: Uses pre-trained unimodal encoders.
Applies adversarial cross-modal latent alignment.
Learns shared representations with minimal paired samples.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports evaluation on niche classification and cell type composition prediction, plus release of an annotated three-organ dataset with paired images and gene expression.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no numerical performance estimates or external clinical validation, limiting assessment of effect size and generalizability.
infographic.paper_title: Learning Multimodal Representations from Partially Paired, Small-Scale Data

title: Leakage-Free Is Not Confounder-Free: What a Patient-Level Split Cannot Certify About a Medical Imaging Benchmark
authors: Ignazio Gallo, Mattia Gatti, Leonardo Sgroi, Darwin Castillo, Yuliana Jiménez-Gaona, Nicola Landro
abstract: Patient-level splitting is the standard safeguard against subject leakage in medical imaging evaluation, but it cannot remove a confounder that every fold inherits: an acquisition variable aligned with the diagnosis across the whole cohort. We present a five-question audit of a candidate confounder: how well it predicts the diagnosis, whether it can be decoded from the images, whether diagnostic scores depend on it, whether the image adds predictive value beyond it and how much discrimination survives once it is controlled. We apply it to DMR-IR, the public dataset on which most machine-learning results in breast thermography rest. On 236 patients under a strict patient-disjoint protocol, the acquisition date alone predicts malignancy at AUROC 0.980, above every imaging arm we evaluated (best 0.949), because benign and malignant patients were recruited in different years. The acquisition year is decodable from the pixels among patients who share a diagnosis, largely through a global thermal offset outside the breast, yet only one arm, the one pooling every frame of a visit, demonstrably carries it into its diagnostic score. No arm improves on the date on paired folds, and once the date is controlled, discrimination either collapses or survives only on comparisons the benchmark cannot attribute. The dataset contains only eight cross-label same-date pairs, from ten patients, which limits reliable evaluation within recorded acquisition-date groups. A second, independently acquired cohort, whose dominant channel is patient age, reproduces every finding except legibility, from a confounder that is clinically legitimate. Mitigation may suppress such a confounder, but without cross-label acquisition support no evaluation on the benchmark can certify that what remains is pathology.

infographic.key_insight: Patient-level splits prevent subject leakage but cannot rule out diagnostic predictions driven by acquisition-related confounders shared across folds.
infographic.clinical_relevance: High benchmark accuracy alone may not establish that a medical imaging model detects pathology rather than differences in how patients were recruited or scanned.
method: Audit whether a candidate confounder predicts diagnosis and can be decoded from images.
Test whether model scores depend on the confounder and whether images add predictive value beyond it.
Measure discrimination after controlling for the confounder.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 236 DMR-IR patients with patient-disjoint evaluation, acquisition date predicted malignancy at AUROC 0.980 versus 0.949 for the best imaging arm; no imaging arm improved on date alone in paired folds.
infographic.watch_item: Only eight cross-label same-date pairs from ten patients were available, limiting reliable evaluation within acquisition-date groups and attribution of residual performance to pathology.
infographic.paper_title: Leakage-Free Is Not Confounder-Free: What a Patient-Level Split Cannot Certify About a Medical Imaging Benchmark

title: MedUIGym: Evaluating and Training GUI Agents for Clinical Workflows
authors: Yitong Qiao, Lei Liu, Yue Shen, Jian Wang, Jinjie Gu, Zhixuan Chu
abstract: Automating clinical workflows requires vision-language agents that can navigate dense graphical user interfaces (GUIs) in electronic health records (EHRs) and execute precise actions, yet many medical agents still rely on text or structured tool calls. In this work, we introduce MedUIGym, a scalable interactive environment comprising 15,739 tasks from 17 benchmark sources across six clinical task families for training and evaluating clinical GUI agents. In MedUIGym, agents perceive EHR states from screenshots and execute mouse-and-keyboard actions, as well as a paired native-tool interface over identical clinical data. The environment verifies both final answers and required clinical actions, and supports parallel trajectory collection for training. Benchmarking twelve vision-language models shows that current agents struggle across diverse clinical workflows, and simply increasing reasoning effort fails to yield consistent gains. Furthermore, MedUIGym supports offline learning from GUI trajectories and online reinforcement learning from task rewards. After training, both Qwen3.5 models perform better on in-domain clinical tasks and generalize to tasks from external sources. By unifying tasks from existing benchmarks, dual-interface evaluation, and GUI trajectory collection, MedUIGym provides a testbed for studying how vision-language agents complete clinical tasks through the EHR's graphical interface. Our project page is available at https://github.com/yitong-qiao/MedUIGym.

infographic.key_insight: MedUIGym provides a testbed for clinical GUI agents, showing that current models struggle with EHR workflows but can improve through task-specific training.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The platform supports research on agents that navigate EHR screens and execute workflow actions, rather than only generate text.
method: Agents use screenshots and mouse-and-keyboard actions, with a paired native-tool interface over identical clinical data.
Evaluation checks both final answers and required clinical actions.
GUI trajectories and task rewards support offline learning and online reinforcement learning.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 15,739 tasks from 17 benchmark sources and six clinical task families, evaluation of 12 vision-language models found workflow difficulties; training improved both Qwen3.5 models on in-domain and external-source tasks.
infographic.watch_item: Benchmark improvements do not establish safety or reliability in live clinical EHR workflows.
infographic.paper_title: MedUIGym: Evaluating and Training GUI Agents for Clinical Workflows

title: Virtual spatial transcriptomics links kidney histopathology to disease-associated molecular programs
authors: Nonchev, K.; Jang, Y.; Nlandu Khodo, S.; Koelzer, V. H.; Raetsch, G.; Moor, M. B.
abstract: IntroductionSpatial transcriptomics can resolve compartment-specific molecular programs in kidney disease, but its cost and technical requirements limit its use in clinical diagnostics and in large biopsy archives. Predicting spatial gene expression from routine histology with artificial intelligence could extend molecular characterization to existing clinically annotated kidney tissue collections. MethodsWe adapted DeepSpot-M, a pretrained multimodal foundation model that predicts spatial gene expression from histology, using paired hematoxylin and eosin images and Visium spatial transcriptomics from 209 Kidney Precision Medicine Project (KPMP) participants. We evaluated virtual profiles in held-out human biopsies, associated them with histopathologic and biochemical injury markers in 567 rats with defined nephrotoxin exposures from a public toxicogenomics database, and generated a virtual atlas from 1 534 histology slides of 476 additional KPMP participants. ResultsKidney-specific adaptation of DeepSpot-M doubled the mean Pearson correlation of each models 1 000 best-predicted genes (0.43 versus 0.22) and exceeded recent foundation models. Virtual profiles preserved the direction of all 13 disease-marker differences in measured expression, including tubular injury, maladaptive repair, gluconeogenesis, and fibrosis-associated programs. All 11 measured associations between molecular programs and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) were also preserved. Without rat-specific training, a virtual injury score distinguished moderate or severe histopathologic lesions (area under the curve, 0.85) and at least twofold blood urea nitrogen elevation (0.82). In our atlas of 5.46 million virtual spots, higher proximal tubule program scores were associated with higher eGFR (partial r, 0.32) and less interstitial fibrosis (-0.57), and program-pathology associations agreed with those of measured Visium profiles in independent participants (Spearman{rho} , 0.64). ConclusionsKidney-adapted virtual spatial transcriptomics links histology-derived molecular programs to experimental renal injury and human clinical and histologic phenotypes. Our approach enables spatial molecular analyses in routine biopsy histology, which could help decipher disease-associated pathways in existing biopsy archives. Translational StatementSpatial molecular profiling of kidney biopsies is informative but too costly for routine use, whereas hematoxylin and eosin sections exist for nearly every biopsy. We show that a model adapted to paired kidney histology and spatial transcriptomics infers programs of tubular injury, metabolic differentiation, and fibrosis from routine histology, and that these programs track kidney function and pathology across 476 participants. Applied to existing archives, virtual spatial transcriptomics could stratify heterogeneous patients by tissue molecular state, prioritize biopsies for targeted assays, and support biomarker discovery and trial enrichment once validated prospectively.

infographic.key_insight: Kidney-adapted AI predicted spatial gene-expression programs from routine histology, doubling mean correlation for the 1,000 best-predicted genes from 0.22 to 0.43.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Virtual molecular profiling could extend research on kidney injury and fibrosis to archived biopsies without requiring spatial transcriptomics for every sample.
method: Adapted DeepSpot-M using paired H&E images and Visium profiles from 209 KPMP participants.
Evaluated held-out human biopsies and injury associations in 567 nephrotoxin-exposed rats.
Generated an atlas of 5.46 million virtual spots from 1,534 slides across 476 additional participants.
infographic.evidence_signal: Predictions preserved all 13 tested disease-marker differences and all 11 tested eGFR associations; rat injury discrimination reached AUCs of 0.85 for moderate/severe lesions and 0.82 for at least twofold blood urea nitrogen elevation.
infographic.watch_item: Predicted expression is not a direct molecular measurement, and the abstract does not establish prospective clinical utility or generalizability across routine pathology settings.
infographic.paper_title: Virtual spatial transcriptomics links kidney histopathology to disease-associated molecular programs

title: SAE-Audit: Clinical-Trial Prediction via Inference-Time Optimization of Black-Box LLMs Audited by Sparse Autoencoder Evidence
authors: Junbo Shen
abstract: Clinical trials are costly and often take years to complete, making early outcome prediction valuable for trial planning. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to forecast clinical-trial outcomes, yet their predictions remain unreliable and their rationales may not faithfully reflect the evidence underlying their answers. On tasks such as predicting whether a registered clinical trial will complete or terminate early, frontier LLMs perform only modestly above chance in our experiments. We introduce SAE-Audit, which optimizes a black-box LLM at inference time with evidence obtained from a deployable open model. A frozen sparse autoencoder (SAE) on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct is converted into a vocabulary of clinical concepts. Sparse probes fitted on past trials determine which concepts are associated with the outcome. For a new protocol, the concepts detected by the probe are written as evidence, each with the direction and strength of its association with the outcome, and the LLM being audited optimizes its answer in the light of this evidence. Without additional training, SAE-Audit raises balanced accuracy of deepseek-v4-flash by 9.6--12.0 points on five clinical-trial prediction tasks and raises GPT-5.6-terra by 8.0 points on trial completion, exceeding other agentic inference-time optimization methods by a large margin. As an auxiliary, SAE probes module within SAE-Audit is itself accurate and auditable, providing natural-language explanations directly derived from verified concept contributions and protocol evidence, without requiring additional LLMs at inference time. SAE-Audit provides verifiable, concept-level evidence for more accurate and auditable clinical-trial prediction. It can also be embedded into biomedical AI agents such as Biomni to optimize their performance.

infographic.key_insight: SAE-Audit improves black-box LLM predictions of clinical-trial outcomes by supplying auditable, concept-level evidence during inference.
infographic.clinical_relevance: More reliable forecasts of trial completion or early termination could support trial planning, though prospective utility is not established.
method: Convert a frozen sparse autoencoder on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct into a vocabulary of clinical concepts.
Fit sparse probes on past trials to identify outcome-associated concepts and their contribution strengths.
Provide protocol-specific concept evidence to a black-box LLM to refine its prediction without additional LLM training.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports balanced-accuracy gains of 9.6–12.0 percentage points for deepseek-v4-flash across five prediction tasks and 8.0 points for GPT-5.6-terra on trial completion.
infographic.watch_item: Concept associations are not causal explanations, and the abstract does not specify sample sizes or prospective validation.
infographic.paper_title: SAE-Audit: Clinical-Trial Prediction via Inference-Time Optimization of Black-Box LLMs Audited by Sparse Autoencoder Evidence

title: CT-Navigator: Towards Interpretable and Generalizable CT Understanding through Agentic Perception and Tool-Invocation
authors: Yibing Fu, Huidong Xie, Yihao Niu, Wei Ji, Heming Dong, Ziyue Wang
abstract: Clinical computed tomography (CT) interpretation inherently requires progressive visual exploration, where radiologists navigate from whole scans to individual slices and regions of interest and interact with external tools when necessary. However, existing 3D medical multimodal large language models (MLLMs) typically connect a specialized 3D visual encoder to a language model, without fully leveraging the native 2D visual and agentic capabilities of generalist MLLMs. Trained on large-scale one-hop CT instruction-following data, these models also have limited ability to perform iterative reasoning and explicitly ground their conclusions in visual evidence, limiting their support for traceable CT interpretation. To solve these problems, we propose \textbf{agentic perception} as an alternative paradigm inspired by radiologists' interpretation workflows. We introduce \textbf{CT-Navigator}, a framework that harnesses generalist MLLMs' 2D visual and agentic capabilities to progressively ground CT interpretation in explicit, traceable visual evidence through hierarchical visual exploration and radiology tool invocation. To build these capabilities, we curate 8,904 visual chain-of-thought (V-CoT) trajectories for cold-start agentic supervised fine-tuning. We then optimize the policy through reinforcement learning on 33,219 questions, with data selection and dynamic rollout sampling prioritizing informative learning signals. Finally, we introduce CTNavi-Bench, a 3D CT visual question answering benchmark comprising 7,000 questions spanning anatomical regions throughout the human body. CT-Navigator achieves 79.50\% accuracy on CTNavi-Bench, surpassing the strongest baseline by 17.59\%, and demonstrates strong generalization across three external CT benchmarks. The code, model, and benchmark will be released on \href{https://github.com/fyb99/ct_navigator}{GitHub}.

infographic.key_insight: CT-Navigator uses progressive visual exploration and tool invocation to ground CT question answering in traceable image evidence rather than one-step scan interpretation.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could support more inspectable CT interpretation workflows, but clinical utility and safety are not established by the reported benchmarks.
method: Uses a generalist multimodal model to navigate CT scans hierarchically, from whole scans to slices and regions of interest.
Invokes radiology tools and learns from 8,904 visual chain-of-thought trajectories.
Refines its policy with reinforcement learning on 33,219 questions, prioritizing informative training signals.
infographic.evidence_signal: On the new 7,000-question CTNavi-Bench, CT-Navigator achieved 79.50% accuracy, with a reported 17.59% improvement over the strongest baseline, and showed generalization across three external CT benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: Benchmark accuracy and traceable outputs do not establish reliable clinical reasoning; prospective validation and tool-error assessment remain important.
infographic.paper_title: CT-Navigator: Towards Interpretable and Generalizable CT Understanding through Agentic Perception and Tool-Invocation

title: When Should We Trust Medical Image Models? Evaluating Confidence Reliability under Cross-Dataset Shift
authors: Haoran Zhang, Sarah Lam, Yuting Lin, Nuo Chen, Mingyang Li
abstract: Deep learning models for chest X-ray analysis often achieve strong performance on benchmark datasets, but their reliability under cross-dataset deployment remains unclear. In clinical practice, models trained in one hospital system may be applied to data from another, where distributional and labeling differences can affect both prediction accuracy and model confidence. We conduct a controlled empirical study of model confidence under cross-dataset transfer. We train ResNet-50 and DenseNet-121 on CheXpert and evaluate them on MIMIC-CXR across five experimental settings, focusing on Pneumothorax and Pleural Effusion. We measure predictive performance using AUC and confidence reliability using Expected Calibration Error (ECE), Brier score, and average confidence on incorrect predictions, all reported with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. We further evaluate post-hoc temperature scaling fit on the source validation set and use Grad-CAM to examine the mechanism behind cross-domain performance differences. Cross-domain AUC drops 7-13 percentage points, and the best in-domain model is not the best cross-domain model. Source-domain temperature scaling produces marginal ECE changes but systematically increases confidence on incorrect predictions across all four model-pathology combinations. Grad-CAM reveals that DenseNet relies on a concentrated spatial prior that fails to transfer, while ResNet's more distributed attention generalizes better. These findings argue for cross-site validation and safety-specific calibration metrics in medical AI evaluation.

infographic.key_insight: Under cross-dataset shift, chest X-ray models lost predictive performance, and source-fitted temperature scaling increased confidence in incorrect predictions.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Strong benchmark performance and calibrated source-domain confidence may not indicate reliable predictions at another hospital.
method: Trained ResNet-50 and DenseNet-121 on CheXpert and evaluated transfer to MIMIC-CXR.
Assessed pneumothorax and pleural effusion using AUC, ECE, Brier score, and confidence on incorrect predictions.
Tested source-validation temperature scaling and examined attention patterns with Grad-CAM.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across five experimental settings, cross-domain AUC dropped 7–13 percentage points; metrics were reported with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals.
infographic.watch_item: Evidence covers two architectures, two pathologies, and one transfer direction; broader reliability requires validation across additional sites and tasks.
infographic.paper_title: When Should We Trust Medical Image Models? Evaluating Confidence Reliability under Cross-Dataset Shift

title: Toward a digital twin of the ICU patient: Forecasting and treatment response in a generative event model
authors: Zhuoyang Lyu, Yiming Li, Peter C. Hou, Pengyu Hong, Li Zhou
abstract: A digital twin of a patient in intensive care would forecast the patient's course and what a treatment would change. Generative event models, trained to continue a patient's electronic health record (EHR), have been proposed as a path toward such twins. We trained TWICE, a 79M-parameter decoder-only transformer, on the ICU records of one academic health system (127,332 training patients and 1.57 billion tokens). We evaluated it on clinical prediction tasks, generation fidelity, individual trajectories and counterfactual validation. Reading 19 clinical outcomes off 50 simulated futures, with no task-specific training, TWICE matched the best of 144 supervised configurations on held-out patients (mean AUROC 0.836 vs. 0.834). It led on events that change care within a day and trailed on death. With the training data fixed, more and longer simulated futures were worth more than a 6.8-fold larger model. Its generated records matched real ones closely and were as specific to each patient as its own variability allowed. Its predicted risk rose as events approached. Pre-specified controls showed that it reproduced the side effects of drugs and was barely moved by an inert drug. On the values that treatments are given to correct, however, an opposite treatment moved its forecasts like the right one. TWICE forecasts ICU events about as well as task-specific models, and we see it as a step toward a digital twin of the ICU patient.

infographic.key_insight: TWICE forecast ICU outcomes comparably to task-specific models, but its treatment-response errors limit its readiness as a patient digital twin.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Simulated patient futures could support ICU risk forecasting, but the results do not establish reliable predictions of treatment benefit.
method: Trained a 79M-parameter decoder-only transformer to continue ICU electronic health records.
Estimated 19 outcome risks from 50 simulated futures without task-specific training.
Evaluated record fidelity, patient trajectories and counterfactual treatment responses.
infographic.evidence_signal: Trained on 127,332 patients and 1.57 billion tokens from one academic health system, TWICE achieved mean AUROC 0.836 on held-out patients versus 0.834 for the best of 144 supervised configurations.
infographic.watch_item: Opposite treatments shifted forecasts similarly on measures they were intended to correct, raising concerns about causal validity for treatment simulation.
infographic.paper_title: Toward a digital twin of the ICU patient: Forecasting and treatment response in a generative event model

title: A Cascaded Framework with a Cross-Attention-Guided Mamba-CNN Model for Pre- and Post-Treatment Glioma Segmentation
authors: Siavash Taremi, Mahmoud Heidari, Seyed Mohammad Hossein Hashemi, Mohsen Hooshmand
abstract: Accurate glioma segmentation is vital for diagnosis and follow-up, but manual segmentation is time-consuming, subjective, and variable across interpreters. Gliomas are heterogeneous in size, shape, and location. Deep learning has therefore emerged as a potential solution. CNNs excel at local features but may struggle with long-range dependencies, whereas Vision Transformers capture global context efficiently but incur higher computational complexity. Most previous studies focused on pre-treatment gliomas; post-treatment cases with resection cavities (RCs) remain less explored. This study proposes a Cross-Attention-Guided Mamba-CNN (CMC-Seg) model within a cascaded framework for pre- and post-treatment diffuse glioma segmentation, aiming to balance accuracy and computational cost. Experiments used BraTS 2025 mpMRI of diffuse glioma patients. After preprocessing, a coarse segmentation model extracted tumor-centered patches, which were fed to CMC-Seg for fine-grained segmentation. CMC-Seg was compared with 3D U-Net, SegResNet, SwinUNETR, UNETR, nnFormer, and SegMamba. On the test set, CMC-Seg achieved the highest mean Dice (81.20%) and non-enhancing tumor core (NETC) Dice (77.09%). It also achieved an RC Dice of 78.63% and the lowest 95% Hausdorff distance (HD95; 4.39 mm). Results were comparable to CNN and Mamba baselines and significantly better than Transformer-based baselines (P < 0.05). CMC-Seg required the fewest inference GFLOPs (381.49). Ablation experiments indicated that multi-direction scanning and cross-attention improved performance, particularly for RC (P < 0.05). Grad-CAM explainability experiments showed that CMC-Seg focuses on diagnostically relevant tumor regions.

infographic.key_insight: CMC-Seg combined CNN and Mamba features with cross-attention, achieving the highest reported mean Dice (81.20%) and lowest inference GFLOPs (381.49) among tested models.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Automated segmentation could support glioma assessment before and after treatment, including resection cavities, but clinical utility remains unproven.
method: A coarse segmentation model extracted tumor-centered patches from multiparametric MRI.
CMC-Seg used cross-attention-guided Mamba and CNN features for fine-grained segmentation.
Ablation studies assessed multi-direction scanning and cross-attention.
infographic.evidence_signal: On the BraTS 2025 test set, CMC-Seg achieved 77.09% non-enhancing tumor core Dice, 78.63% resection cavity Dice, and 4.39 mm HD95; performance was comparable to CNN/Mamba baselines and significantly better than Transformer baselines (P < 0.05).
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not report external clinical validation, so generalizability beyond the benchmark remains uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: A Cascaded Framework with a Cross-Attention-Guided Mamba-CNN Model for Pre- and Post-Treatment Glioma Segmentation

title: KMed-31B Technical Report
authors: KMed Team
abstract: We present KMed-31B, a medical large language model post-trained from an open-weight model for on-premises deployment with limited hardware. Post-training a model for diverse medical tasks remains difficult, because improving one kind of task can lower performance on another. We attribute this to differences between tasks in expected output and available feedback. Medical question answering and diagnosis prediction have reference answers, whereas clinical inquiry has no single correct response and is judged with rubrics. We therefore divide medical training tasks into four categories by these two properties, train one specialist per category with a reward that its feedback supports, and integrate the specialists into a single student with Multi-teacher On-policy Delta Distillation (MOPD$^2$). For clinical inquiry, we build Synthetic Health Dialogue, a simulated corpus of consultations with lay users and clinicians whose patient cases span common clinical presentations in primary care. Relative to its base model, KMed-31B raises HealthBench Hard from 22.95 to 41.87 and HealthBench Professional from 37.92 to 50.20 in non-thinking mode, and from 23.80 to 51.48 and from 41.97 to 59.18 in thinking mode, while its scores on four multiple-choice medical benchmarks are maintained or slightly improved. KMed-31B has the highest unadjusted HealthBench Hard score among the compared models, including proprietary ones, and scores higher on HealthBench Professional than every open-weight model we compare, including models with more than ten times as many total parameters. Applied to another base model, Qwen3.8-27B, the same training recipe also raises both HealthBench scores. We describe the training recipe, data construction, and settings in detail so that institutions requiring on-premises deployment can develop medical models from open-weight foundations.

infographic.key_insight: KMed-31B combines task-specific medical specialists into one model, improving clinical dialogue benchmarks while maintaining or slightly improving medical multiple-choice scores.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach targets institutions seeking on-premises medical AI, but benchmark gains do not establish safety or effectiveness in patient care.
method: Divide medical tasks into four categories by expected output and available feedback.
Train a specialist for each category and integrate them using Multi-teacher On-policy Delta Distillation (MOPD²).
Build Synthetic Health Dialogue from simulated patient–clinician consultations spanning common primary care presentations.
infographic.evidence_signal: Relative to its base model, thinking-mode HealthBench Hard rose from 23.80 to 51.48 and Professional from 41.97 to 59.18; four medical multiple-choice benchmark scores were maintained or slightly improved.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports benchmark evaluation rather than prospective clinical validation and does not quantify hardware requirements for on-premises deployment.
infographic.paper_title: KMed-31B Technical Report

title: Synthetic EHR Generators Should Be Audited Like LLMs
authors: Inigo Stibbe, Padmanabhan Ramnarayan, A. Aldo Faisal
abstract: Synthetic electronic health record (EHR) generation is increasingly adopting large autoregressive models, yet privacy evaluation has not kept pace, relying heavily on similarity-based heuristics and aggregate metrics that can obscure patient-specific memorisation. We argue that these models should additionally undergo LLM-style memorisation audits at the level of individual patient records. We support this position by comparing membership-inference evaluations across four prominent autoregressive EHR generators, highlighting inconsistent evaluation practices in patient representations and attack procedures. We evaluate trajectory reconstruction from partial context and introduce randomly assigned patient-level canaries to distinguish memorised associations from clinical generalisation. We examine these methods in a GPT-2-style model deliberately overfit to 1,000 MIMIC-IV patient trajectories, creating a controlled setting in which memorisation should be readily detectable. The model systematically recovers training patients' canaries, and their trajectory reconstruction approaches perfect accuracy with increasing context. Held-out patients show no systematic canary recovery, while reconstruction remains low and improves only marginally with additional context. These experiments establish a positive-control baseline for further evaluation of these methods in realistically trained models.

infographic.key_insight: Autoregressive synthetic EHR generators should undergo patient-level memorisation audits alongside aggregate privacy evaluations.
infographic.clinical_relevance: These audits could reveal patient-specific privacy risks that similarity-based checks and aggregate metrics may miss.
method: Compare membership-inference evaluation practices across four autoregressive EHR generators.
Test patient-trajectory reconstruction from partial context.
Use randomly assigned patient-level canaries to separate memorisation from clinical generalisation.
infographic.evidence_signal: In a GPT-2-style model deliberately overfit to 1,000 MIMIC-IV patient trajectories, training-patient canaries were systematically recovered and reconstruction approached perfect accuracy as context increased, unlike held-out patients.
infographic.watch_item: This deliberately overfit positive-control experiment does not establish privacy risk or audit performance in realistically trained models.
infographic.paper_title: Synthetic EHR Generators Should Be Audited Like LLMs

title: The AMPEL Platform: An Open-Source Project for Developing Hospital-Wide Clinical Decision Support Systems under EU-Regulation
authors: Alexander Twrdik, Daniel Steinbach, Martin Federbusch, Clemens Malkawi, Maria Schmidt, Toralf Kirsten
abstract: As incentives to digitize more and more aspects of medical healthcare are gaining traction, additional medical data is becoming available. A major goal is to use this data to gain further insights, support medical staff, and ultimately improve patient care. This demands sophisticated solutions that can handle current and future vast amounts of data, all without disrupting well-established workflows of care takers. Additionally, the solution must fulfill the documentation and risk-management obligations of the Medical Device Regulation (MDR), which governs whether a device may be used in patient care in Europe. In this context, we introduce the AMPEL platform, an open-source solution for creating clinical decision support systems (CDSS) that fulfil the requirements of the MDR. Centered around a message broker (Kafka), it adopts an event-driven, distributed architecture, allowing for scaling and efficient processing of medical data as it gets generated. Relying on platform-specific events to implicitly describe the platform's interfaces makes it both extensible and agnostic to the hospital information system in use. With these events being defined in the Protocol Buffers format, medically evaluated algorithms can be independently implemented in a variety of programming languages and easily linked to the platform, extending its analytic capabilities as desired. The platform features a basic UI and alert functionality that can be used to gain medical staff's attention and present analysis results in a traceable and explainable fashion. We further show in a use case how the platform was used to build LAMPE, a CDSS developed and operated at University of Leipzig Medical Center. It demonstrates how the platform solution can be used in a complex and already established environment, while acknowledging current limitations and outlining planned developments to overcome these.

infographic.key_insight: AMPEL is an open-source platform designed to build hospital-wide clinical decision support systems while supporting EU Medical Device Regulation requirements.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The platform aims to deliver traceable, explainable alerts and analysis results to medical staff without disrupting established care workflows.
method: Uses Kafka-based, event-driven distributed architecture to process incoming medical data.
Defines platform events with Protocol Buffers to connect independently developed algorithms across programming languages.
Provides a basic user interface and alert functionality for presenting results.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract describes implementation through LAMPE at University of Leipzig Medical Center but reports no quantitative performance or patient-outcome evaluation.
infographic.watch_item: Platform adoption alone does not establish regulatory compliance or clinical benefit; deployment requires local validation and risk management.
infographic.paper_title: The AMPEL Platform: An Open-Source Project for Developing Hospital-Wide Clinical Decision Support Systems under EU-Regulation

title: Leakage-Safe Auditing of Attribution-Driven Data Curation in Medical Imaging
authors: Malay Phadke, Akshay Gokhale
abstract: When can an attribution-derived anomaly justify changing a medical-imaging training set? We formulate attribution-driven curation as three separately testable claims: anomaly detection, harmfulness estimation, and intervention utility. We test the first and third using a patient-disjoint, identifier-preserving audit of a 3D convolutional classifier for computed tomography angiography aneurysm candidates. We identify 232 exactly zero-valued arrays among 1,201 positive patches, including 170 training positives, and invalidate a historical 321-patch attention-failure subgroup whose identifier-free records were joined to files by position. On the held-out test set, GradCAM++ spatial concentration is central for every candidate class, reversing the historical pattern. GradCAM++ and Integrated Gradients show negative rank-order agreement for positives, limiting method-independent anatomical interpretation. Across five paired training seeds, removing the 170 corrupted training positives yields AUC 0.9617 +/- 0.0044 versus 0.9652 +/- 0.0039 for full-data training (difference -0.0035; 95% CI -0.0082 to 0.0007). Excluding 34 raw-zero test positives widens rather than closes the gap, countering a blank-memorization explanation. Budget-matched random-removal controls suggest the result is not simply an effect of reducing training size. Input corruption does not necessarily imply that deletion improves generalization. Our framework makes leakage control, sample identity, and intervention testing explicit in attribution-driven medical-imaging data curation.

infographic.key_insight: Detecting corrupted medical-imaging inputs does not establish that removing them improves model generalization.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Medical-imaging AI curation should validate sample identity and test downstream performance rather than treat attribution anomalies as sufficient grounds for deletion.
method: Separated anomaly detection, harmfulness estimation, and intervention utility into testable claims.
Audited a 3D CTA aneurysm-candidate classifier using patient-disjoint data and preserved identifiers.
Compared full-data training with corrupted-positive removal across five paired seeds and budget-matched random-removal controls.
infographic.evidence_signal: The audit found 232 zero-valued arrays among 1,201 positive patches; removing 170 training positives yielded AUC 0.9617 versus 0.9652 with full data (difference −0.0035; 95% CI −0.0082 to 0.0007).
infographic.watch_item: Negative rank-order agreement between GradCAM++ and Integrated Gradients for positives limits method-independent anatomical interpretation.
infographic.paper_title: Leakage-Safe Auditing of Attribution-Driven Data Curation in Medical Imaging

title: Decompose and Describe: Narrowing the Diagnosis-to-Report Gap in 3D CT Report Generation
authors: Zhisong Wang, Wanxing Chang, Weiwei Cao, Fenghe Tang, Bowen Shi, Ruifeng Yuan
abstract: Automated 3D CT report generation could support radiology workflows, yet medical vision-language models (MedVLMs) often omit diagnostic findings from generated reports. We ask whether the diagnostic ability of these models carries over to free-form reporting. Across five MedVLMs, diagnostic VQA achieves higher macro-F1 than reports generated from the same CT studies and evaluated on the same disease categories. We call this task-dependent discrepancy the diagnosis-to-report gap. Conventional Report Adaptation improves reporting for most models but does not close the gap. To investigate and narrow it, we introduce DeCAD (Decompose CT Analysis and Describe), which progressively decomposes CT report generation at diagnostic, regional textual, and regional visual levels. The model identifies positive findings before writing a report, organizes diagnosis and description into regional tasks, and restricts each task to visual tokens from the corresponding region. Diagnostic and regional textual decomposition improve report-level diagnostic performance across the five MedVLMs, whereas regional visual decomposition provides limited additional gains. In a standard VLM without medical VQA pretraining, the first two levels remain effective; regional visual decomposition also provides further gains with a region-level contrastively pretrained encoder. Full DeCAD achieves state-of-the-art performance on CT-RATE and Merlin. Analyses show greater CT-token attention during diagnosis and higher recall of reference-positive findings in both the diagnostic output and final report than with Report Adaptation. These results show that explicitly organizing diagnosis improves diagnostic reporting and helps narrow the diagnosis-to-report gap.

infographic.key_insight: Medical vision-language models recognize CT findings better in diagnostic Q&A than in free-form reports; DeCAD narrows this diagnosis-to-report gap.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Explicitly organizing diagnosis before report writing could help reduce omitted CT findings, but clinical benefit remains unproven.
method: Identify positive findings before drafting the report.
Organize diagnosis and description into anatomical-region tasks.
Restrict each regional task to its corresponding CT visual tokens.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across five medical vision-language models, diagnostic Q&A outperformed reporting on macro-F1; full DeCAD achieved state-of-the-art performance on CT-RATE and Merlin.
infographic.watch_item: Regional visual decomposition added limited gains in medical models, and benchmark improvements do not establish real-world clinical safety.
infographic.paper_title: Decompose and Describe: Narrowing the Diagnosis-to-Report Gap in 3D CT Report Generation

title: Ontology-Compiled 2D Clinical State Fields with Bidirectional Diffusion Encoders for Zero-Training Cross-Ontology Medical Coding
authors: Zeqiang Wang
abstract: Healthcare systems continually revise clinical taxonomies, update reimbursement schedules, and harmonize cross-border registries. Existing automated coding models bind clinical text understanding to fixed vocabulary-specific heads, requiring manual relabeling and retraining whenever code sets change. We introduce Ontology-Compiled 2D Clinical State Fields (OCSF), a vocabulary-free framework that decouples clinical document reading from target ontology indexing so one trained encoder can switch across arbitrary medical vocabularies in seconds without target training. A single-pass bidirectional diffusion-pretrained encoder and vocabulary-free decoder map each clinical note into a fixed-dimension two-dimensional state matrix with zero code-specific parameters. Any target ontology is compiled offline on CPU from public text descriptions into a scale-invariant Tikhonov deconvolution operator that suppresses sibling-code interference while preserving source decision thresholds. Trained solely on English MIMIC-IV ICD-9 discharge summaries and evaluated without target tuning across 58,706 held-out test notes and five unseen ontologies spanning English ICD-10, MS-DRG, Spanish, Greek, and Chinese (115-185,458 codes), OCSF reaches 63.15% Micro-F1 on in-domain ICD-9 (outperforming a matched closed-vocabulary classifier and eliminating late-epoch tail overfitting) and transfers directly to 26,085 English ICD-10 codes (29.23% recall at gold cardinality), MS-DRG groups, and multilingual terminologies, compiling up to 185,458 codes in under 10 seconds on CPU with sub-millisecond GPU readout.

infographic.key_insight: OCSF separates clinical-note encoding from ontology indexing, allowing one trained model to switch medical code sets without target-specific training.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could reduce retraining burdens when coding standards change, though real-world coding accuracy and workflow value remain to be established.
method: Encode each note into a fixed-size 2D clinical state matrix without code-specific parameters.
Compile ontology descriptions offline into a Tikhonov deconvolution operator to reduce interference between sibling codes.
Apply the compiled operator to read out codes without target-specific tuning.
infographic.evidence_signal: Trained only on English MIMIC-IV ICD-9 discharge summaries, OCSF was evaluated across 58,706 held-out notes and five unseen ontologies, reporting 63.15% in-domain Micro-F1 and 29.23% recall at gold cardinality for English ICD-10.
infographic.watch_item: Recall measured using the true number of codes per note does not establish performance when that number is unknown in routine coding.
infographic.paper_title: Ontology-Compiled 2D Clinical State Fields with Bidirectional Diffusion Encoders for Zero-Training Cross-Ontology Medical Coding

title: Beyond Fidelity: Evaluating Synthetic Medical Imaging Data
authors: Seyed Kahaki, Alexander R. Webber, Tahsin Rahman, Elim Thompson, Jana Delfino, Aldo Badano
abstract: The growing use of synthetic medical imaging datasets (SMD) in the development and evaluation of machine learning models has motivated interest in systematic methods to assess dataset quality across different imaging modalities. Common evaluation strategies rely heavily on fidelity-oriented metrics developed for general computer vision and may not capture clinically relevant properties such as anatomical plausibility, dataset coverage, metadata completeness, subgroup consistency, or documentation quality. We present the ScoreCard Toolkit that operationalizes six of the seven dimensions found within the 7Cs approach for SMD evaluation across Congruence, Coverage, Completeness, Consistency, Constraint, and Comprehension. The ScoreCard Toolkit provides a modular pipeline for preprocessing, feature extraction, metric computation, visualization, and structured scorecard generation. This approach complements standard fidelity-based evaluation by exposing quality characteristics not captured by those measures alone, including constraint violations, anatomically implausible shape artifacts, and metadata-related consistency issues. The toolkit supports appearance, texture, and shape features and is designed to accommodate additional feature representations, including radiomic features, deep-learning embeddings, and foundation-model representations. We demonstrate the end-to-end workflow across three imaging modalities: synthetic digital pathology whole-slide image patch data, synthetic digital mammography, and synthetic head CT. Across all three modalities, the resulting scorecards reveal dataset-specific quality characteristics, such as distributional biases and coverage gaps that may impact their effectiveness for model development or testing. ScoreCard provides a practical, extensible, and modality-agnostic approach for evaluating and transparently reporting SMD quality.

infographic.key_insight: The ScoreCard Toolkit evaluates synthetic medical imaging data beyond visual fidelity, revealing anatomical, distributional, and metadata-related quality issues.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Broader quality checks may help researchers identify synthetic-data weaknesses that could affect medical imaging AI development and testing.
method: Operationalizes six dimensions: Congruence, Coverage, Completeness, Consistency, Constraint, and Comprehension.
Combines preprocessing, feature extraction, metric computation, visualization, and structured scorecards.
Supports appearance, texture, and shape features, with extensibility to additional representations.
infographic.evidence_signal: Demonstrations on synthetic pathology patches, mammography, and head CT revealed dataset-specific distributional biases and coverage gaps.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports no quantitative validation linking scorecard findings to downstream model performance or clinical outcomes.
infographic.paper_title: Beyond Fidelity: Evaluating Synthetic Medical Imaging Data

title: Foundation Model and Radiomics Distance Scores for Post-Hoc Segmentation Failure Detection
authors: Simon Johannes Joham, Gianluca Guglielmo, Mateusz Kozinski, Martin Urschler
abstract: Medical image segmentation models can fail silently when clinical data differs from training data. Deployed models rarely ship with quality control, and are often black boxes. Prior methods that work in this post-hoc failure detection setting still need a separate regression or segmentation model, registration, or access to model internals. We instead propose two failure scores based on the Mahalanobis distance to a labeled reference set. The first uses radiomic shape features of the predicted mask. The second uses frozen foundation model (FM) features, made mask-aware by overlaying the mask on the image, encoding it with a frozen DINOv3, and pooling patch features with more weight on the mask region. We test on multi-site prostate and hippocampus MRI under imaging-protocol and population shift. Ranking cases by predicted failure risk within each site, both scores are competitive with the registration-based (Atlas-RCA) and ensemble-based (pairwise Dice) baselines, without registration that can fail silently or access to individual predictions. Our results show that pooling all test cases into one ranking, as prior work does, rewards ordering sites by difficulty, so a detector can rank sites well, miss failures within them, and still look strong. Within-site evaluation measures true per-case failure. The two evaluation schemes reward different behavior, so we recommend reporting both. The code is available at https://github.com/imigraz/fm-radiomics-failure-detection.

infographic.key_insight: Radiomic shape and frozen foundation-model distance scores can flag segmentation failures post hoc, while within-site evaluation reveals errors that pooled rankings may obscure.
infographic.clinical_relevance: These scores could support quality-control review of prostate and hippocampus MRI segmentations when deployed models are black boxes.
method: Measure Mahalanobis distance from predicted-mask radiomic shape features to a labeled reference set.
Overlay masks on images, encode with frozen DINOv3, and use mask-weighted patch pooling to compute a second distance score.
Rank cases by failure risk without registration or access to segmentation-model internals.
infographic.evidence_signal: On multi-site prostate and hippocampus MRI under protocol and population shifts, both scores were competitive with Atlas-RCA and ensemble pairwise-Dice baselines for within-site ranking.
infographic.watch_item: Report both pooled and within-site performance: strong pooled rankings can reflect site difficulty rather than reliable detection of individual failures.
infographic.paper_title: Foundation Model and Radiomics Distance Scores for Post-Hoc Segmentation Failure Detection
